audience.programmeDescription: Maastricht studies Europe through history, politics, international relations, law, economics, philosophy and sociology. Students develop research skills and complete a thesis or Final Project.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The closest UCR option connects European institutions and law with history, economics and society. The second applies law and policy to climate and sustainability. Maastricht offers more dedicated European Studies coursework and a required final research component.

curriculum.limitation: This example uses the first-listed options in the restricted choice groups. The 24 EC elective semester remains open.

componentNotes.y2-07: Choose one of EU Law II, External Relations of the EU, or Challenges in Contemporary Democracies.

componentNotes.y3-01: Combine approved electives, a minor, study abroad or an internship for 24 EC.
componentNotes.y3-03: Thesis students choose one 4 EC methods course. This example uses Interviewing.
componentNotes.y3-05: Two examiners assess the final work. Students may instead take the 21 EC Final Project, which has limited places and replaces the thesis and methods course.

notes.text: Maastricht offers dedicated courses on European identity, economic integration, diplomacy and Central and Eastern Europe, alongside a sequence of research workshops. UCR combines EU law and politics with broader disciplinary courses.

The UCR options emphasise either European institutions and society or European climate policy. Maastricht’s final semester includes either a thesis with a separate methods course or a larger Final Project.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

BENECON111.name: Introduction to Economics
BENECON111.text: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.

BENECON211.name: International Macroeconomics
BENECON211.text: Study the economy as a whole through topics such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment. Understand how governments and central banks use fiscal and monetary policies to influence economic performance over time. The course also explores business cycles, international trade, and economic crises, preparing students to evaluate policy debates and global economic trends.

BENECON311.text: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.text: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.

BENLEAD312.name: Negotiation & Strategic Thinking
BENLEAD312.text: How do you get to yes? In this course you will learn how to craft persuasive arguments, deploy the right language, negotiate more effectively, and influence decisions with confidence—whether in business, leadership, or life.

ENSDELT312.name: Governance of Sustainability
ENSDELT312.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.

ENSENVI112.text: Covers geoscience principles and analytical tools to understand natural disasters. Compares risks from climate change‑driven events and mining disasters and teaches actions to reduce risks from events like earthquakes, droughts and toxic algae blooms.

Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and study chemical and physical principles relevant to climate, energy and materials. A laboratory project makes and tests starch-based biopolymers.

Case briefs, demand letters and mock trials develop legal reasoning, while a family-law topic supports the design of a socio-legal research proposal.

MCCCOMM112.name: Dutch
MCCCOMM112.text: This course aims to develop basic skills and strategies necessary to successfully handle uncomplicated oral and written communication in Dutch in a variety of social situations that you may encounter in daily life in the Netherlands. The emphasis in the course will be on speaking in Dutch in day-to-day situations on the one hand and understanding Dutch culture on the other hand. At the end of the course students can orally express and write about themselves in Dutch, who they are, describe their family background, and interact with others in a simple way.
